# Least squares estimation

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The least squares criterion {.smaller}

The [residual]{style="color: tomato;"} for each day is the difference between the observation and the model prediction. The least squares criterion is the [sum of squared residuals]{style="color: tomato;"}, the [SSE]{style="color: steelblue;"}

::: {style="color: steelblue;"}
$$\text{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(y_i - f(t_i, \theta)\bigr)^2$$
:::

- [$y_i$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is the observation on day [$t_i$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
- [$f(t_i, \theta)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is what the model predicts for that day with parameters [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"}

The parameters that make this sum smallest are the [least squares estimates]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Properties of the squared error criterion

- Squaring makes every residual positive, so residuals above and below the curve do not cancel
- Large residuals are [penalised much more heavily]{style="color: tomato;"} than small ones
- The SSE is a [differentiable]{style="color: tomato;"} function of [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, which gradient-based optimisers rely on
- Under normally distributed errors with constant variance ([homoscedasticity]{style="color: tomato;"}), the least squares estimate is also the [maximum likelihood estimate]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Limitations of the squared error criterion

- The criterion is [sensitive to outliers]{style="color: tomato;"}: a single extreme observation can pull the whole fit towards itself
- It [assumes constant variance]{style="color: tomato;"}, treating a day with 3 pupils in bed the same as a day with 300, which count data rarely satisfy
- It has [no probabilistic interpretation]{style="color: tomato;"}, so it provides no measure of uncertainty on its own

------------------------------------------------------------------------

- If you had to report one number from this fit with a straight face, which would it be?

## Strengths of least squares {.smaller}

- [Computationally cheap]{style="color: tomato;"}, with well-established optimisation algorithms available in every statistical package
- An [intuitive]{style="color: tomato;"} criterion that is easy to explain and to implement
- Under its assumptions the estimates are [unbiased]{style="color: tomato;"}, with the [minimum variance]{style="color: tomato;"} among linear unbiased estimators
- Good [initial values]{style="color: tomato;"} for the likelihood-based methods that follow, which is how we use it in the next section

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Limitations of least squares {.smaller}

- [No uncertainty quantification]{style="color: tomato;"}: the objective function surface was visibly tilted and elongated, but the point estimate carries none of that information
- [No principled basis for model comparison]{style="color: tomato;"}
- The [constant variance assumption]{style="color: tomato;"} is violated by count data, whose variance grows with the mean
- [Parameter identifiability]{style="color: tomato;"} problems are not diagnosed, only hidden in the shape of the surface

------------------------------------------------------------------------
